newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: No unified Americas military position on drugs war.
newsitem.headline: No unified Americas military position on drugs war.

text.p: Military mobilisation in Latin America's war against drugs should remain a national decision and not become a unified continental operation, Americas defence chiefs decided on Wednesday.

"We established each country should take into account its own needs and circumstances to resolve whether it involves its armed forces or not," said Colombian Defence Minister Juan Carlos Ezguerra Portocarrero, whose forces are deeply involved in the fight against Colombia's drug cartels.

"Colombia has no choice but to commit its armed forces. But inside Colombia the fight is Colombia's. Each country's military should work on its own, while cooperating with the others," he told reporters at the end of three days of talks.

Defence chiefs from 32 Western Hemisphere nations -- including the United States and Canada, but excluding Cuba -- decided the scale of the drug problem varied so much from country to country there could be no unified position.

Mercosur trading partners Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay insisted with Chile and Mexico that the fight against "narco-terrorism" was the realm of the civilian police, though the military could provide logistical support.

Chilean Defence Minister Edmundo Perez Yoma, whose country is one of the least affected by the drug problems of its coca-producing neighbours Peru and Bolivia, told Reuters, "the issue of drugs affects countries in the region differently. In the case of Chile, we insisted we don't want our armed forces directly involved in combatting the drugs trade."

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who left the conference late on Tuesday, insisted on the need for a regional fight against drugs and supported Panama's proposal to provide a coordination base, possibly linked to Howard Air Base in the United States.

"One of the greatest difficulties in dealing with and fighting the narcotics traffic is that each nation deals with this problem as a national problem," Perry said on Monday, underlining U.S. military help for Colombia and Venezuela in operation Laser Strike to develop radars to catch drug smugglers.
But he insisted that in such cases the military acted "in support of law enforcement agencies ... not functioning as a law enforcement agency."

The United States cites "narco-terrorism" as one of the reasons that Latin America's armed forces need to modernise their hardware. Washington is reviewing its ban on sales of high-tech lethal weaponry to Latin America in recognition of the spread of democracy in the region.

But some Latin countries with recent memories of border conflicts are nervous at the prospect of neighbours acquiring modern U.S. weapons. Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez expressed concern that Chile's interest in buying 15 U.S. F-16 fighters risked touching off a regional arms race.
Perry's assurances sales would be on a case-by-case basis and take into account the subordination of armed forces to democratic civilian rule helped ease fears.
"Our countries are calm about it. The commitment to transparency will help and it's clear that in South America and specifically the southern zone there is no arms race," Chile's Yoma told reporters.
